title: Ezekiel 13:1–16
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Israel’s prophets who speak out of their own heart, saying “The LORD says” when the LORD has not sent them. They are like foxes among ruins; they have not repaired the gaps in the wall, and they have promised peace when there is no peace. Their message is pictured as whitewash on a flimsy wall that will collapse in a storm of the LORD’s wrath, exposing both the wall and those who plastered it. Jeremiah also condemns prophets who cry “Peace, peace” (Jeremiah 6:14; 8:11). Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about testing claims to speak for God.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel. A message against false prophets begins.

Arminian readers see God protecting his people by exposing those who mislead them, so that the people can recognize and reject false words.
verses.reformedNotes:
The chapter follows naturally from 12:24, which promised an end to false vision and flattering divination.

Reformed readers see God guarding the integrity of his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the importance of distinguishing true and false prophecy.

verses.text: “Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who prophesy, and say to those who prophesy out of their own heart, ‘Hear the LORD’s word:
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to prophesy against Israel’s prophets who prophesy “out of their own heart.” Their source is their own imagination.

Arminian readers see prophets responsible for presenting their own ideas as God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah 23:16 speaks similarly of prophets who “speak a vision of their own heart.”

Reformed readers see the danger of human words passed off as divine. Both traditions read this as shared ground about testing claims to speak for God.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says, “Woe to the foolish prophets, who follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing!
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD pronounces woe on the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and have seen nothing. Their visions are empty.

Arminian readers see accountability for those who claim revelation they did not receive.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Foolish” here implies moral and spiritual failure, not mere lack of intelligence.

Reformed readers see God exposing false claims. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of misrepresenting God and the harm it does to those who trust such words.

verses.text: Israel, your prophets have been like foxes in the waste places.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel’s prophets have been “like foxes in the waste places.” The image suggests scavenging in ruins.

Arminian readers see prophets who exploit a crisis rather than serve the people in it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image may suggest creatures that thrive among ruins or that undermine what remains; readers offer both senses.

Reformed readers see self-serving leaders. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the precise sense of the image loosely.

verses.text: You have not gone up into the gaps or built up the wall for the house of Israel, to stand in the battle in the LORD’s day.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophets have not gone up into the gaps or built up the wall to stand in battle on the LORD’s day. They failed to protect the people.

Arminian readers see a failure to call the people to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Repairing the gaps may picture calling the people back to God before judgment; compare 22:30.

Reformed readers see failed spiritual leadership. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the prophet’s duty to warn and strengthen God’s people.

verses.text: They have seen falsehood and lying divination, who say, ‘The LORD says;’ but the LORD has not sent them. They have made men to hope that the word would be confirmed.
verses.arminianNotes:
They have seen falsehood and lying divination, saying, “The LORD says,” though the LORD has not sent them, and they have made people hope for fulfillment. False hope is the harm.

Arminian readers see people misled by confident claims.
verses.reformedNotes:
Using “The LORD says” without being sent is the core of the charge.

Reformed readers see the gravity of false authority. Both traditions read this as shared ground about testing claims made in God’s name.

verses.text: Haven’t you seen a false vision, and haven’t you spoken a lying divination, in that you say, ‘The LORD says;’ but I have not spoken?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks whether they have not seen a false vision and spoken a lying divination, saying “The LORD says” when he has not spoken. The charge is direct.

Arminian readers see the prophets confronted with their own words.
verses.reformedNotes:
The rhetorical question leaves no room for excuse.

Reformed readers see God exposing those who misuse his name. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the integrity required of anyone who claims to speak for God.

verses.text: “ ‘Therefore the Lord GOD says: “Because you have spoken falsehood and seen lies, therefore, behold, I am against you,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Because they have spoken falsehood and seen lies, the Lord GOD says he is against them. God opposes false prophecy.

Arminian readers see judgment responding to deliberate misrepresentation of God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase “I am against you” marks a solemn declaration of opposition.

Reformed readers see God defending his truth. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s opposition to those who speak lies in his name, which harms his people and dishonors him.

verses.text: “My hand will be against the prophets who see false visions and who utter lying divinations. They will not be in the council of my people, neither will they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, neither will they enter into the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
God’s hand will be against the false prophets: they will not be in the council of his people, nor written in Israel’s register, nor enter the land. They lose their place.

Arminian readers see consequences matching their misuse of trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
The register likely refers to a record of the community’s members, though its exact nature is uncertain.

Reformed readers see exclusion from the covenant community. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hedge the register’s nature.

verses.text: “ ‘Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, “Peace;” and there is no peace. When one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash.
verses.arminianNotes:
They have seduced God’s people, saying, “Peace;” when there is no peace, like those who whitewash a flimsy wall. The image is cover-up.

Arminian readers see false assurance keeping people from repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah 6:14 and 8:11 also condemn those who say “Peace, peace” when there is no peace.

Reformed readers see comforting lies masking danger. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Tell those who plaster it with whitewash that it will fall. There will be an overflowing shower; and you, great hailstones, will fall. A stormy wind will tear it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to tell the whitewashers that the wall will fall under rain, hailstones, and stormy wind. The cover-up will fail.

Arminian readers see false security unable to withstand reality, as the coming judgment will show.
verses.reformedNotes:
The storm imagery pictures judgment exposing what the whitewash hid.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment revealing truth. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the failure of reassurances that do not rest on God’s word.

verses.text: Behold, when the wall has fallen, won’t it be said to you, “Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it?”
verses.arminianNotes:
When the wall falls, people will ask, “Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it?” The prophets will be exposed.

Arminian readers see the false prophets answerable to those they misled.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question carries a note of mockery at the failed reassurance.

Reformed readers see God vindicating his true word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the accountability of those who offer false comfort and the eventual exposure of their message.

verses.text: “ ‘Therefore the Lord GOD says: “I will even tear it with a stormy wind in my wrath. There will be an overflowing shower in my anger, and great hailstones in wrath to consume it.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD will tear the wall with a stormy wind, an overflowing shower, and hailstones in his wrath. Judgment comes from God.

Arminian readers see God acting against a people who embraced false security.
verses.reformedNotes:
The storm imagery of verse 11 is now attributed directly to God.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s action in exposing falsehood and the seriousness of his anger against lies told in his name.

verses.text: So I will break down the wall that you have plastered with whitewash, and bring it down to the ground, so that its foundation will be uncovered. It will fall, and you will be consumed in the middle of it. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will bring down the whitewashed wall to its foundation, and they will be consumed in it; then they will know he is the LORD. The collapse is complete.

Arminian readers see consequences falling on those who built on lies.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image shifts from the wall to those inside it.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment exposing every false foundation. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of trusting false reassurances rather than God’s word.

verses.text: Thus I will accomplish my wrath on the wall, and on those who have plastered it with whitewash. I will tell you, ‘The wall is no more, nor those who plastered it—
verses.arminianNotes:
God will accomplish his wrath on the wall and those who whitewashed it, and say, “The wall is no more, nor those who plastered it.” God’s word over the wall is final.

Arminian readers see judgment ending false comfort.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse joins the wall and the whitewashers under the same judgment.

Reformed readers see God’s justice complete. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the end of false security.

verses.text: to wit, the prophets of Israel who prophesy concerning Jerusalem, and who see visions of peace for her, and there is no peace,’ ” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The whitewashers are the prophets who see visions of peace for Jerusalem when there is no peace. The image is explained.

Arminian readers see prophets responsible for misleading the city in its final years.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse makes explicit that the false prophets are the plasterers of the image.

Reformed readers see God identifying those who mislead his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the harm done by visions of peace that God did not give.
